title: Functions
description: Function declaration, definition, prototypes, parameters, return values, call-by-value, recursion, and scope.
objectives: Declare and define functions, and understand prototypes

content.heading: Declaration, Definition, and Prototypes
content.body: A function definition provides both its signature and its body: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }. A function prototype (or declaration) provides just the signature, ending in a semicolon with no body: int add(int a, int b); — placed before main() (or in a header file), it tells the compiler about a function's existence and signature before its full definition appears later in the file (or in a separate file entirely), letting the compiler type-check calls to it that appear earlier. Without a prototype, calling a function before its definition appears in the same file is a compile error in modern C (older, pre-C99 compilers were more lenient here, implicitly assuming an int-returning function — a legacy behavior modern code should never rely on).

content.heading: Call by Value, Recursion, and Scope
content.body:
C is strictly call-by-value: every argument is copied into the function's parameter. This means a function cannot directly modify a caller's variable through a plain parameter — to achieve that, the caller must pass a pointer (the variable's address), and the function dereferences it to read/write the original (covered fully in the Pointers lesson).

Recursion works the same as in any language: a base case to stop, and a recursive case that progresses toward it; C has no tail-call optimization guaranteed by the standard, so deep recursion risks a stack overflow. Local variables declared inside a function (or a block within it) have block scope — they exist only within that block and are destroyed when it exits; a variable declared in an outer block is visible in nested inner blocks unless shadowed by a same-named inner declaration.

content.explanation: The prototype for add() lets main() call it before its full definition appears further down the file. factorial demonstrates a base case (n <= 1) and a recursive case that shrinks n toward it.

keyPoints: A prototype (signature + semicolon) lets a function be called before its full definition appears
C is strictly call-by-value — a plain parameter cannot modify the caller's original variable
Every recursive function needs a base case; C has no guaranteed tail-call optimization
Local variables have block scope, existing only within the block that declares them
commonMistakes: Calling a function before its prototype or definition is visible, causing a compile error
Expecting a function to modify a caller's variable through a plain (non-pointer) parameter
Omitting a recursive function's base case, causing unbounded recursion and a stack overflow
